clinicalPearls: Congenital diverticula are typically solitary, occur near the ureteric orifice (Hutch diverticulum) and have otherwise normal detrusor; acquired diverticula are usually multiple and arise secondary to bladder outlet obstruction with a trabeculated bladder.
The diverticular wall is deficient in organised detrusor muscle, so it empties poorly and predisposes to stasis, recurrent infection and stone formation.
A large Hutch diverticulum adjacent to the ureterovesical junction can distort the antireflux mechanism and cause vesicoureteric reflux or functional ureteric obstruction.
Post-void residual urine within the diverticulum produces a characteristic pattern of double micturition or a sensation of incomplete emptying.

Urinary stasis carries a recognised risk of malignancy within the diverticulum, most often urothelial carcinoma but with a relatively higher proportion of squamous cell and adenocarcinoma than in the main bladder.
Because the diverticular wall lacks a muscle layer, any tumour arising within it can invade beyond the bladder early, worsening the stage at presentation.
Voiding cystourethrography and cross-sectional imaging define the neck, size and relationship to the ureters and guide whether diverticulectomy is needed.
Management of acquired diverticula must address the underlying outlet obstruction, otherwise diverticula recur or symptoms persist after excision.
reference.pathophysiology: A bladder diverticulum is a herniation of bladder urothelium and lamina propria through a defect or weakness in the detrusor muscle, producing an outpouching whose wall contains little or no organised muscle. Congenital diverticula reflect a primary focal weakness of the detrusor, classically at the ureterovesical junction (Hutch diverticulum), and occur in an otherwise normal, non-obstructed bladder. Acquired diverticula develop when chronically raised intravesical voiding pressure, most often from bladder outlet obstruction (benign prostatic obstruction, urethral stricture or neurogenic dysfunction), forces mucosa between hypertrophied detrusor bundles of a trabeculated bladder. Because the diverticulum contracts poorly, urine pools within it during and after voiding; the resulting stasis underlies recurrent infection, calculus formation and an elevated long-term risk of malignant transformation of the diverticular urothelium.
additionalDifferentials: Bladder outlet obstruction with detrusor trabeculation and sacculation
Vesicoureteric reflux with a dilated distal ureter
Bladder ear (transient extraperitoneal herniation in infants)
Patent processus or inguinoscrotal bladder herniation
additionalInvestigations: Voiding cystourethrography to demonstrate the diverticular neck and any vesicoureteric reflux
CT urography or MRI to define size, wall, ureteric relationship and detect intradiverticular tumour
Cystoscopy to inspect the diverticular neck and interior for tumour and calculi
Urodynamic study to confirm and characterise outlet obstruction or detrusor dysfunction
Renal function assessment and upper tract ultrasound
redFlags: Visible haematuria or positive cytology suggesting malignancy within the diverticulum
A solid filling defect or enhancing mass inside the diverticulum on imaging
New hydronephrosis or deteriorating renal function from ureteric compression or reflux
Recurrent urosepsis or a large retained infected residual
Rapidly enlarging diverticulum causing bladder outlet or ureteric obstruction
reference.prognosis: Small asymptomatic diverticula with the underlying obstruction relieved carry an excellent outlook and can be observed. Prognosis worsens substantially when malignancy arises within a diverticulum, because the muscle-deficient wall permits early extravesical spread and a more advanced stage at diagnosis.
pitfalls: Excising the diverticulum without relieving the causative outlet obstruction, leading to recurrence or persistent symptoms
Overlooking an intradiverticular tumour because the diverticular interior is difficult to inspect fully at cystoscopy
Failing to recognise the close relationship to the ureter, risking ureteric injury during diverticulectomy
Attributing incomplete emptying solely to the diverticulum when concurrent detrusor underactivity is present
Assuming all diverticula are acquired and missing a congenital Hutch diverticulum in a child with reflux
references: European Association of Urology Guidelines on non-neurogenic male lower urinary tract symptoms
management: Relieve the underlying bladder outlet obstruction — treating benign prostatic obstruction, urethral stricture or neurogenic dysfunction — as the basis of acquired diverticula
Diverticulectomy for large or symptomatic diverticula and those complicated by recurrent infection, calculi or poor emptying
Ureteric reimplantation where a Hutch diverticulum distorts the ureterovesical junction and causes reflux or obstruction
Treat associated complications, clearing diverticular stones and managing recurrent urinary infection
Cystoscopic surveillance for malignancy within the diverticulum, given stasis-related risk and early extravesical spread
Observe small asymptomatic diverticula once the underlying obstruction is relieved
